body:
I have a proposed fix on [this branch]. It uses the existing `auth.IsTenancy` helper to recognise `*.ghe.com` remotes and includes a regression test covering both HTTPS and SSH GHE remotes.

I'd be more than happy to raise a PR if the team agrees with this approach.

[this branch]: https://github.com/JackMyers001/github-cli/tree/fix-ghe-remote-resolution

**Duplicate check:** Searched for `ghe.com`, "known GitHub host", and GHES/tenancy remote-resolution issues. Found related-but-distinct reports: #12179 (`gh pr checkout` fails when remote host differs from API host) and #14344 (SSH URL construction for `.ghe.com`), but no existing issue covering this exact `GH_TOKEN` + `.ghe.com` remote-resolution failure. No duplicate found.

**Analysis:** I'm suggesting `bug`, `priority-2`, and `gh-auth`. The reproduction is clear and the reporter's fix (setting `GH_REPO`) is consistent with a remote-resolution failure rather than a token problem. My hypothesis: when only `GH_TOKEN` is set (no `GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN`), [`AuthConfig.HasEnvToken`](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/e316a01d277884a839a3b9f2286163d920ddffbf/internal/config/config.go#L288-L307) probes with a synthetic non-github, non-tenancy hostname (`"example.com"`), which routes through go-gh's `tokenForHost` enterprise-token branch and therefore never sees `GH_TOKEN`. As a result `HasEnvToken()` returns `false` even though `GH_TOKEN` is set, so [`remoteResolver.Resolver()`](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/f236c7efab99f2f18a816b4b504864ce3130484a/pkg/cmd/factory/remote_resolver.go#L82-L92) falls through past the `HasEnvToken()` branch to the generic "none of the git remotes ... point to a known GitHub host" error instead of the more specific "set the GH_HOST environment variable" message - and separately, the `.ghe.com` tenant subdomain remote may not match any host in the resolver's `hosts` set if it isn't already an authenticated host, causing `FilterByHosts` to drop it. This would explain why explicitly setting `GH_REPO` (which bypasses remote-based host resolution) works around the problem. Confirming this needs a maintainer trace through `remoteResolver` with a `.ghe.com` remote and `GH_TOKEN` set but no `gh auth login` session, to pin down whether the failure is in `HasEnvToken`, host-set construction, or `FilterByHosts` matching.

body:
Hey @JackMyers001,

Thanks for the super detailed report. I think I understand what's going on here. I assume that if you set `GH_HOST=tenant.ghe.com` (in place of `GH_REPO`) that it would resolve this as well, maybe you can double check that.

That said, I'm a bit surprised we haven't heard this before, so will need to dig a little deeper!

<!-- ai-flow:impact -->
Yes, setting `GH_HOST` in the above workflow also works, it's just slightly more hardcoding 😉. I've just run a test on my GHEC instance to confirm.

Ok I've refreshed my memory on this and I'm in two (or three, or four) minds. The current state of the design is broadly:
 1. Collect the hosts in the git remotes
 2. Filter out any hosts we don't know about (either via `gh auth login`, `GH_REPO`, or `GH_HOST`, or github.com)

Historically, the reason for the second step is to avoid sending a token to the wrong host. Consider the following hypothetical:

**Given** I have `GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN` set in my environment, that is for GHES host `my-ghes.com`
**And** given my `cwd` is a git repository with a remote pointing to `your-ghes.com`
**When** I run `gh issue list`
**Then** the token in my environment is sent to the wrong host?

In the case of `GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN`, we require the caller to explicitly state the desired host as part of the command through `GH_HOST` or `GH_REPO`.

Now when we're looking at GHEC, the same shape of hypothetical problem can occur:

**Given** I have `GH_TOKEN` set in my environment, that is for GHEC host `my.ghe.com`
**And** given my `cwd` is a git repository with a remote pointing to `your.ghe.com`
**When** I run `gh issue list`
**Then** the token in my environment is sent to the wrong host?

On the other hand, even **today** this is an issue:

**Given** I have logged into `your-ghes.com` via `gh auth login`
**Given** I have `GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN` set in my environment, that is for GHES host `my-ghes.com`
**And** given my `cwd` is a git repository with a remote pointing to `your-ghes.com`
**When** I run `gh issue list`
**Then** the token in my environment is sent to the wrong host

The stored login makes the host eligible for remote selection, then `GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN` overrides its stored token.

The same issue is also apparent with automatically recognising `github.com`:

**Given** I have `GH_TOKEN` set in my environment, that is for GHEC host `my.ghe.com`
**And** given my `cwd` is a git repository with a remote pointing to `github.com`
**When** I run `gh issue list`
**Then** the token in my environment is sent to the wrong host

All round, `GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN` (and `GH_TOKEN` for `ghe.com`) kind of sucks. Not requiring a [clear host and token mapping](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/12928) has been a significant pain point the last few years.

I'm not exactly sure where to go from here. I could make an argument that we should require `GH_HOST` or `GH_REPO` to avoid expanding this. On the other hand, I could make an argument that if you have two `ghe.com` hosts in git repos, you probably have some reasonable level of trust in the hosts.

Thanks for digging into this! I appreciate the detailed response. I understand why the existing host filter matters, and fully agree that an explicit host-to-token mapping would make this clearer and more secure.

> Filter out any hosts we don't know about (either via `gh auth login`, `GH_REPO`, or `GH_HOST`, or `github.com`)

I'd argue GHEC tenant domains should also count as known hosts. The [environment docs] group `github.com` and subdomains of `ghe.com` together for `GH_TOKEN` / `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and describe `GH_HOST` as specifying the hostname when one cannot be inferred from the local repository. Reading those together, I'd expect a checkout with a single `tenant.ghe.com` remote and a matching `GH_TOKEN` to just work.

On the wrong-host scenarios, I think the important distinction is who operates the receiving host. If a `GH_TOKEN` (which is only ever used for GitHub.com and GHEC hosts) is sent to the wrong tenant or instance, this doesn't seem like a problem: the host is GitHub-operated, the request is rejected, and the user gets an auth error. The dangerous case is a `GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN` being sent to a remote on `evil-ghes.com`, where an attacker could harvest it.

All my change does is allow `GH_TOKEN`s to be used on GHEC remotes, as is the documented/expected behaviour. This does allow a `GH_TOKEN` to reach a different `ghe.com` tenant than intended, which mirrors the existing `github.com` behaviour you described. GHES hosts still only become eligible through a stored login, `GH_HOST`, or `GH_REPO`.

The change itself is one small addition: hosts that `auth.IsTenancy` recognises are added to the eligible set, and credential selection and `GH_HOST` filtering are untouched. I also wrote some (AI-assisted) matrix tests covering github.com, two GHEC tenants and a GHES host across every combination of environment tokens and stored credentials. They confirm cloud and enterprise tokens never cross over, that `GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN` alone with only cloud remotes still fails before any request is made, and that the two-tenant case behaves as described above.

Would you be open to a PR for automatic recognition of GHEC remotes now, with the explicit mapping tracked separately? If you'd rather require `GH_HOST` for `GH_TOKEN` on GHEC, I think that the docs should be updated to clarify this, since at the moment they read as though inference from the local repository should work.

[environment docs]: https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_help_environment

> On the wrong-host scenarios, I think the important distinction is who operates the receiving host. If a GH_TOKEN (which is only ever used for GitHub.com and GHEC hosts) is sent to the wrong tenant or instance, this doesn't seem like a problem: the host is GitHub-operated, the request is rejected, and the user gets an auth error.

I agree this is an important distinction, and it already has precedence as above:

**Given** I have `GH_TOKEN` set in my environment, that is for GHEC host `my.ghe.com`
**And** given my `cwd` is a git repository with a remote pointing to `github.com`
**When** I run `gh issue list`
**Then** the token in my environment is sent to the wrong host

I suppose my concern is that the more we loosen the constraint, the more likely we are to leak something unexpectedly. On the other hand, when I initially decided to use `GH_TOKEN` for `ghe.com` hosts, I did so because I wanted users to be able to lift and shift their actions workflows from github.com to ghe.com without friction, and this is definitely friction.

I think I'm open to accepting a change here, but since it is security sensitive I'll want to get buy in from the team.

Thanks, that makes sense. Happy to wait for the team's view and use the workaround I've identified for now. If the team decides to go ahead, could you add the `help-wanted` label so I can open a PR from my branch?
